ACBE: Swaps following an index of autocallable notes, structured products that pay regular income from stock market exposure and can end early when markets cooperate. This version aims for core portfolio income with a steadier profile than the high income variant, at the cost of lower payouts.
ACBH: Swaps that follow an index of autocallable notes, structured products on stock markets that pay high income and can end early in calm markets. It is built for maximum payouts from that note design, which means capped gains and losses if markets fall hard.
AHD: A portfolio of autocallable notes tied to Robinhood stock, structured products that pay high income while the stock behaves and can end early. If Robinhood falls hard and stays down, the notes can lose sharply, so the income carries real risk.
BFEW: A ladder of four buffer funds on equal-weighted large US stocks, each with its own one-year protection period staggered through the year. The laddering smooths the timing risk of buying a buffer on the wrong day, in exchange for capped gains throughout.
BNAV: Bitcoin exposure run tactically: the fund leans in when price trends look healthy and pulls back toward safety when they break down. The signal-driven approach aims for fewer deep crashes than plain bitcoin, accepting it can be caught out by sudden reversals.
BSGT: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2029, so the fund behaves like a single government bond with a known end date. It suits savers aiming at a late-decade goal, paying government-backed interest without company credit risk.
BSTV: US Treasury bonds that all mature in 2031, bundled so the fund ends like a single government bond. It is built for a goal in the early 2030s, paying government-backed interest with a known finish line and no company credit risk.
BZZ: Drone makers and the young air taxi industry: companies building unmanned aircraft and the services around them, mostly industrial firms. It is a speculative bet on skies filling with delivery drones and flying taxis, so expect sharp swings.
CABZ: Self-driving car and robotaxi companies: the firms building driverless vehicles, their sensors and software, split between technology and consumer names. It is a bet on rides without drivers becoming normal, a futuristic theme that swings on regulation and testing news.
CIEI: US Treasury bonds with three to seven years left until they mature, the middle ground of government debt. It pays steady interest with moderate price swings when rates move, steadier than long bonds but more rewarding than cash-like funds.
CIVG: Corporate bonds from solid, investment-grade companies with one to five years until they mature. Short maturities keep price swings small, so it works as a steadier income holding that pays a bit more than government bonds of similar length.
CMBO: An interest rate strategy that shifts its bets as rates move, using derivatives to profit from rising or falling yields while keeping maturities very short. It aims to make money from rate swings themselves rather than simply collecting steady interest.
CMCI: Raw materials across energy, metals and farm goods, reached through contracts tied to a broad commodity index that spreads bets across delivery dates. The steady-maturity approach aims for smoother commodity exposure than funds concentrated in the nearest futures contracts.
DGLO: US companies set to gain as supply chains come home: manufacturers and industrial firms are 60 percent of the fund, with energy producers behind. It is a bet on factories, chips and goods being made in America again instead of overseas.
DINE: Income from many sources at once: dividend stocks, bonds, option spreads and currency trades, arranged with taxes in mind. The tax-aware mix aims to keep more of each payout after tax, which sets it apart from ordinary income funds.
EMEM: Emerging market companies picked by Sophus Capital's managers, led by Asian technology firms such as chipmakers, with banks and other industries behind them. It is a growth holding: these markets can grow faster than rich countries but swing harder on politics, currencies and sentiment.
EMTY: A short-term trading tool that rises as brick-and-mortar retail chains fall, betting daily against physical stores. It is built on the idea that online shopping keeps hollowing out malls, but the daily reset makes it unsuitable for holding through rallies.
ETTY: Ether, the second-biggest cryptocurrency, paired with option selling designed to pay out about 3 percent a month in premium income. It keeps part of ether's price moves while harvesting steady premiums, though big ether rallies are partly sold away.
FHIL: Leading companies from outside the US, picked by Federated Hermes across technology, industrials, banks and health care. It is a core international holding of established market leaders, aiming for steadier growth than narrower foreign bets.
FTG: Mid-sized US growth companies picked using behavioral finance, the study of how investor mistakes create mispriced stocks, with technology about half the fund. The managers look for overreactions to buy into, so it hunts bargains inside the growth world.
GALX: Space companies: rocket launchers, satellite makers and the firms supplying them, led by industrials at about 60 percent. It is a growth bet on the business of orbit, from broadband satellites to defense payloads, and swings on launches and contracts.
GNMX: Companies in genomics and precision medicine: firms reading DNA to tailor treatments to each patient, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on medicine becoming personal, swinging on research results, approvals and health care politics.
GRPZ: About 90 small US companies chosen for growth at a reasonable price: strong growers that still score well on quality and value measures. It blends three styles that usually fight each other, aiming for small-cap growth without paying any price.
HJUN: The S&P 500 with a full shield: over the year starting in June, it is designed to protect against the whole of a market fall while capping gains. It offers the strongest cushion in this fund family, in exchange for giving up big rallies.
HUMM: Companies building the power systems for AI data centers: the equipment that delivers high-voltage direct current to racks of AI chips, split between technology and industrial firms. It is a narrow bet on the plumbing behind the AI boom.
KCAI: Large Chinese companies picked by a machine learning process designed to beat the CSI 300 benchmark, with financials the biggest slice at over two-fifths, then industrials and technology. It is a bet on an algorithm outpicking the market, so its holdings can look quite different from the index it chases.
KPRO: Chinese internet companies held through a sister fund plus options designed to protect against the whole of a fall over the period ending in January 2027. In exchange, gains are capped, making it the most defensive way in this family to hold China's internet giants.
LFAO: US Treasury bonds arranged to pay regular income through 2055, designed to fund spending deep into later life. It offers decades of government-backed payments, though prices along the way move with interest rates and the horizon is very long.
LIAE: US Treasury inflation-protected bonds, known as TIPS, arranged to pay steady income that rises with inflation through 2050. It targets later-life spending decades away, protecting buying power over the whole journey rather than chasing the highest payouts today.
LIBD: Treasury inflation-protected bonds set up to pay income through 2065, an unusually long runway aimed at funding spending very late in life. The payments adjust with inflation, so buying power is the priority, though the far-off horizon makes prices rate sensitive.
LQDM: Investment-grade corporate bonds, reached through a big bond fund, plus call options sold every week to target a 12 percent yearly income rate. It turns steady bond holdings into an aggressive payout machine, with the option selling adding risk plain bonds do not have.
MDEV: Medical device companies: the makers of implants, surgical tools, scanners and patient monitors, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on medical technology rather than drug makers, growing with surgeries, aging populations and hospital spending.
MIDE: Mid-sized US companies from the S&P MidCap 400, screened and scored on environmental, social and governance measures to keep about three quarters of each industry. It offers the mid-cap market with an ESG filter, so the heaviest polluters and worst scorers are dropped.
MMAY: The S&P 500 wrapped in an options strategy built to moderate the ride over the year starting in May, cushioning a middle slice of losses. It is a gentler stock holding from Pacer's Swan range, trading some upside for smaller falls.
MUIB: An options strategy on Micron Technology, the memory chip maker, designed to define the outcome in advance and boost income from the stock. It rides on one cyclical chip company, so payouts and prices swing with memory prices and AI demand.
MYY: A short-term trading tool that rises when mid-sized US companies fall, resetting its inverse bet every day. The daily reset steadily erodes value over longer stretches, so it suits brief bearish trades rather than a lasting hedge.
NVPS: The picks and shovels of the Nvidia world: suppliers and partners that sell the chips, cooling, power and parts AI data centers need, rather than Nvidia itself. Technology is over 80 percent, so it rides the AI build-out one step removed.
OWN: One hundred big US companies where insiders, the executives and directors, own the most stock, drawn from the S&P 500. The idea is that leaders with serious money in their own company run it harder, so ownership itself is the selection rule.
PCPC: Property and casualty insurers: the companies that insure homes, cars and businesses against accidents and disasters, making up the whole fund. It is a focused bet on one steady corner of finance, moving with premiums, storms and claims costs.
PQXX: S&P 500 companies wrapped in options that buffer the first 20 percent of losses, with the shield resetting every quarter. The deeper cushion and fast resets suit especially cautious investors, paid for with capped gains each quarter.
QB: The Nasdaq 100 growth giants wrapped in a buffer that adjusts daily, using very short-term options to keep a cushion under the fund as markets move. It aims to keep most of the Nasdaq's upside while softening falls, with the protection rebuilt every day.
RGYY: Weekly income from selling put options on a twice-leveraged fund tied to Rigetti Computing, a quantum computing company. It is an extreme trade: double leverage on a speculative stock means losses can be brutal when the stock falls.
SAWG: Large US companies picked for quality growth: profitable firms with strong track records, led by technology at close to half the fund. Sawgrass's managers favor durable earners over speculative names, aiming for growth with a steadier foundation than most growth funds.
SNPD: Companies with long records of raising dividends, drawn from an S&P dividend aristocrats list and screened further, led by everyday consumer brands, industrials and utilities. It is a steady income holding built on dependable payers rather than the highest yields.
SQBA: S&P 500 companies wrapped in options that buffer the first 15 percent of losses, resetting the shield every quarter. The frequent resets keep protection close to current prices, paid for by capped gains in each quarterly period.
SSMG: Small and mid-sized US growth companies picked by Silvant's managers, spread across technology, industrials and health care. It hunts the next generation of big winners while they are still mid-sized, which means bigger swings than large-company growth funds.
UDI: US companies that pay and grow dividends, chosen with environmental, social and governance screens applied, led by banks and health care. It aims for a high level of income today that can also grow, with the values screen shaping which payers qualify.
USFE: US companies bought with First Eagle's value discipline, spread across health care, technology, media and materials. The managers hunt for solid businesses trading below their worth and hold patiently, aiming to grow money over years while avoiding big losses.
WCMG: Companies from around the world picked by WCM's managers, spread across health care, technology, media and banks. It is a core global holding built on careful stock selection, aiming for durable businesses rather than copying a world index.
XVTS: Tesla stock held directly, combined with options designed to add a target stream of income on top of its price moves. It keeps real exposure to Tesla's rises, unlike pure options funds, but the income program trims the biggest gains.
